claims.text: The Mg-Zn-Cu eutectic additive has a melting range of approximately 340-380 °C.
Adding 2-5 wt% Mg-Zn-Cu powder and sintering at 850 °C produces a transient liquid phase at grain boundaries.
The transient liquid accelerates solid-state diffusion and improves grain-boundary wetting.
Liquid-assisted wetting promotes particle rearrangement and pore elimination through solution-precipitation.
The transient liquid suppresses the formation of coarse, segregated or brittle intermetallic networks.
The transient liquid lowers the activation energy for mass transport.
Liquid-phase-assisted densification can be completed at 850 °C before significant Mg vaporization occurs.
Significant Mg vaporization typically accelerates above 900 °C.
The liquid dissolves segregated transition-metal clusters and reprecipitates them as fine, uniformly distributed precipitates.
The proposed treatment creates a dense, single-phase-like matrix lacking large segregated intermetallics.
The resulting matrix forms a continuous protective oxide scale during subsequent oxidation exposure.
A compact protective oxide layer acts as a diffusion barrier and reduces further oxidation.
Sintering with the additive at 850 °C will produce a relative density greater than 98%.
The 850 °C treatment will reduce oxidation mass gain by more than 40% relative to standard sintered samples.
The 850 °C treatment will limit Mg loss to less than 1 wt%.
Standard solid-state sintering of the same powder at 900 °C without additive typically produces approximately 92% relative density.
Standard solid-state sintering at 900 °C causes significant Mg volatilization and a microstructure dominated by coarse, segregated intermetallic phases.
Below 820 °C, porosity exceeds 5% because liquid-phase mobility is insufficient.
Above 950 °C, Mg loss exceeds 3 wt%.
Changing the transition metal among Zr, Sc and Mn may alter the liquidus temperature and shift the optimum sintering temperature.
